text:
R. c. Cohen

2010 QCCQ 5650

JL1755

COURT OF QUÉBEC

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

« Criminal division »

N° :

500-01-006539-073

DATE :

June 30, 2010

______________________________________________________________________

UNDER THE PRESIDENCY OF : THE
HONORABLE DENIS LAVERGNE, C.Q.J.

______________________________________________________________________

THE QUEEN

Plaintiff

v.

JOSEPH COHEN

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

DECISION

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The defendant responds to three charges arising from an incident that
occurred on May 24, 2007 in the apartment of his uncle Mr. S.C. : assault with
a weapon, assault causing bodily harm and possession of a prohibited device,
contravening to
sections 267a)
,
267b)
and
82 (2)
a) of the
Criminal code
.

I. THE ISSUE

[
2
]

The defendant pleads self-defense under
Article 34(1)
of the
Criminal
code
:

Everyone who is unlawfully assaulted without having
provoked the assault is justified in repelling force by force if the force he
uses is not intended to cause Death or grievous bodily harm and is no more than
is necessary to enable him to defend himself.

II. OUTSTANDING AND RELEVANT FACTS

[
3
]

In March 2006, the plaintiff's father, Mr. S.C., dies. The defendant is
the plaintiff's nephew and the deceased, his grandfather.

[
4
]

In the evidence that the Court holds, there are disputes or
disagreements between the uncle and nephew on the liquidation of the estate and
the cost of maintaining the deceased's grave at the cemetery, particularly the
cost of the flowers.

- Mr. S.C.'s version

[
5
]

The plaintiff said that shortly after the usual period of mourning in
the Jewish relation, the defendant's wife phoned him and asked him to hand in a
cabinet. After that phone call, it was the turn of the defendant to call his
uncle and to show his displeasure while claiming that the cabinet belongs to
him under the provisions for the settlement of the estate.

[
6
]

The plaintiff says he is then without news from his nephew until May 24,
2007.

[
7
]

In the afternoon of May 24, he takes a nap. He woke up at approximately
5:30 p.m. He hears loud knocking at the door of his apartment. He is under
the impression that it is firefighters. Without making sure of whom it is
through the peephole, he opens the doors. Immediately, the defendant hits him
at the temple. His vision blurs. He even believes he sees one or two people
behind the defendant unless it is a double or triple image of him. He claims to
be hit with brass knuckles that he sees in the defendant's hand. He lost
consciousness. He suffered back injuries. He believes he was beaten more than
once.

[
8
]

He phoned the defendant's sister, his niece, for help. It is the husband
of his niece who finally provides first aid. The day after the assault, he went
to the police. Pictures are taken (exhibit P-1). We see the plaintiff's head,
front and profile, blackened left eye, a bandage applied from the brow of the
left eye to the middle of the forehead and redness at the bottom of the left
cheek and near the left ear. The plaintiff says he is now experiencing hearing
problems.

[
9
]

A few days later, it was suggested that he go to the hospital. He sees a
doctor who recommends a scan.

[
10
]

In cross-examination, the plaintiff denies feeling any bitterness
because of the devolution of the estate to his nephew. He denies any discussion
with the defendant to place flowers on the grave of his father. He also does
not remember asking him anything.

[
11
]

He admits he changed his phone number in order, he said, to avoid
talking to the defendant.

[
12
]

In his statement to the police on May 25, he said that the accused
harasses him. This harassment results from the only call mentioned previously.
In fact, it is unclear whether the plaintiff refers to the phone call made in
March 2006 or another call, among others, where he was threatened by the
defendant. This part of the evidence regarding the change of the phone number
and the phone calls is nebulous. In addition, the plaintiff does not remember
when the other phone calls were made; and, he did not report them to the
police. At the trial, he relates the harassment mentioned in his statement to
the issue of flowers.

[
13
]

In that same previous statement made to a police officer, he first maintains
he was beaten several times, then three times for three minutes. At the trial,
he remembers only one strike but said receiving more after he lost
consciousness.

[
14
]

The state in which he finds himself at the time of writing his
statement, less than 24 hours after the assault explains, according to him, the
inconsistency of his comments on the number of blows received.

[
15
]

Although pictures of the back are also taken, none are produced in the
file.

[
16
]

He denies having used a weapon during his nephew's visit. He has none at
home. He admits having walking sticks, stored in a rack at the entrance to the
apartment. These walking sticks are hardwood with metal tips and metal handles.

[
17
]

He has a criminal record. He admits the following charges :

- 1979 :
offence related to impaired abilities and refusal to obey an order from a peace
agent;

- 1984 :
possession of weapon;

- 1986 :
conspiracy to possess a weapon, possession of a prohibited weapon; another
conviction for assault with use of a weapon;

- 1995 :
robbery and use of a firearm which earned him a prison sentence of 18 months;

- 2005 :
intimidation.

- Mr. Joseph Cohen version

[
18
]

The defendant confirms a deterioration of relations with his uncle. He
underlines the disputes and disagreements concerning the estate of the costs of
his grandfather's grave, mainly the cost of flowers.

[
19
]

On May 23, 2007, his uncle calls him and invites him over, the next day,
for a talk regarding the costs of maintenance of the grave of his grandfather
and arrangement is taken for a meeting the day after, at 3:30 pm, at his
uncle's apartment.

[
20
]

As agreed, he goes to his uncle's apartment and calls him from
downstairs. The uncle buzzes him up. He has not seen is uncle in six months. It
is not without some emotion that he sees him again, hoping to find a solution
to reach an agreement that would satisfy one and the other.

[
21
]

The two sit in the living room. His uncle smokes a cigarette and offers
him a glass of water. At one point, his uncle is on phone. They talk about
things and others. But when addressing the issue of costs of maintenance of the
grave or flowers, his uncle shakes and reacts badly when he maintains his
position of refusing to pay more. He puts an end to the discussion and walks to
leave. His uncle walks to and fro in the apartment. He grabs a walking stick,
points it in his direction, striking his hand, and a table. He brandishes it in
his direction.

[
22
]

So, once the conversation gets heated, he puts on his shoes to leave the
apartment. But his uncle, walking sticks in hand, blocks the way to the door.
Faced with the threat of being struck with the walking sticks, incidentally
containing metal components, the defendant grabbed it with his left hand, and
with his right fist, hits his uncle on his head. He collapses to the ground but
held on the defendant's pants, who successfully frees himself and finally
leaves the apartment. From his testimony, one must understand that he did not
use any brass knuckles or something similar.

[
23
]

The defendant explained that his uncle, although he was older, he was born
in 1945, remains at the time of the incident, an individual in good shape. He
was a professional trainer. The defendant, younger, 36 years old at the time,
of good stature and apparently quite vigorous reported a weakness in his leg
following a surgery from which he has not fully recovered.

III. ANALYSIS

[
24
]

The defense of self-defense is one of justification to the extent where
the violence used is not intended to cause death or grievous bodily harm and
that ultimately it is not excessive.

[
25
]

Moreover, the defense of self-defense does not move on to the defendant
any burden of proof. It is up to the prosecutor to prove beyond a reasonable
doubt that the defendant was not acting in self-defense.

[
26
]

In this case, the defendant admits that he struck his uncle. However,
the versions differ diametrically on the circumstances.

[
27
]

The Court does not accept the version of the uncle, Mr. S.C.. This
version does not appear to be likely in view of the context and facts
considered in their entirety :

- if one
sticks to the testimony of Mr. S.C., the defendant appears at his home,
unannounced, to attack him, 14 months after a hostile conversation, he says,
but between the two events he has not had any contact with his nephew about it
or even a discussion : such a scenario simply does not appear credible;

- in his
earlier statement to the police as well as at the trial, he gave three
different versions of the number of blows his nephew gave him, these
heterogeneous versions, whatever the cause, affect its reliability;

- in view of
the pictures on file (exhibit P-1), the visible injuries do not appear
compatible with the many blows Mr. S.C. says or suspects having received nor
with the use of brass knuckles, which given the rather robust constitution of
the defendant, there would be reason to expect more serious injuries; however,
the same injury is better aligned with the version of the defendant according
to which he hit his uncle once at the head;

- because of
the blows, Mr. S.C. claims to have sustained a back injury; pictures taken at
the police station would attest to his injuries. No picture is produced in the
record;

- Mr. S.C.
argues also suffering a hearing loss : there is no evidence of medical nature
on record confirming the fact.

[
28
]

The defendant's version is much more consistent with the context.

[
29
]

The defendant has no reason to go to his uncle's home with no warning,
if their relationships are not good, especially if they are without contact and
without seeing each other for nearly 14 months, as stated by Mr. S.C..

[
30
]

The defendant's version proves much more plausible : if he visits his
uncle in the afternoon of May 24, it is because this one called him the day
before to ask him to pass by to discuss the cost of maintaining the grave of
his grandfather (father of Mr. S.C.).

[
31
]

In addition, Mr. S.C. confirms possessing one or many walking sticks,
stores at the entrance of his apartment. He also corroborates his nephew on the
fact that their relations are somewhat strained since the death of his father.

[
32
]

The Court believes the defendant who says he struck his uncle to stop
him from using his cane. The prosecutor questioned the relevance of the punch
when the defendant is able to neutralize the hand of Mr. S.C. with which he
holds the walking stick. The Court does not agree with this proposal.

[
33
]

First, although more than 25 years younger than him, the defendant is
familiar with his uncle, a trained man, physically capable, engaging in acts of
intimidation against him by striking the walking stick in his hand and then
against the table when he is angry, and when he brandishes the cane in his
direction, he is afraid of being hit.

[
34
]

In this case, it is a reasonable fear based on objective factors. The
defendant believes that gripping and neutralize the hand holding the walking
stick does not mean it would have been impossible for his uncle after a few
seconds to free himself and use it another way.

[
35
]

By all accounts, the defendant has reasonable grounds to apprehend a
threat and believe he cannot escape it except by reacting as he did.

[
36
]

Although it deplores Mr. S.C.'s wounds, the defendant did not use
excessive force. We cannot require that the defendant accurately measure the
amount of force necessary to apply, given the context and circumstances in
which he is. In occurrence, he hit only once. The Court accepts the defense
based on self-defense. In the same breath, the Court for the above reasons does
not believe that the defendant use any brass knuckles.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE
COURT :

ACQUITS

the accused of the three counts of accusation.
